title: So you want to become an MVP? | LIVE176

segments.text: FERNANDA SARAIVA: Hello everyone!
We are here representing MVP program.
I'm Fernanda Saraiva.
I'm the Program Manager, and also responsible
for engaging the amazing product groups with our community.
And I'm followed by Betsy.
BETSY WEBER: Thank you.
I'm Betsy Weber, a Senior Engagement Lead, and I've been
on the MVP team almost 10 years.
With me, we've got --
JEREMY SINCLAIR: I'm Jeremy Sinclair.
I am a Windows Development MVP
and also a Developer Technologies MVP.
PRIYANKA SHAH: And I'm Priyanka
and a Microsoft Foundry MVP and I am coming all the way
over from Australia here.
Arrived yesterday.
FERNANDA SARAIVA: That's awesome.
Thanks everyone.
Welcome. So MVP program is a recognition program
that has been around for 30 years.
Just recognizing the amazing community leaders
that we have around the world.
So right now, we are a little over 4,000, right Betsy?
BETSY WEBER: Yes.
FERNANDA SARAIVA: And tell me a little bit more.
How can an MVP be recognized?
BETSY WEBER: So the MVP Award is Microsoft's way
of saying thank you to the people that give back
in the community, sharing their knowledge freely and openly,
all about the Microsoft products and services.
So we've got about 4,000 MVPs worldwide.
They are in 96 different countries
and speak 49 different languages.
So it truly is a global community.
FERNANDA SARAIVA: And it's really engaging.
Because I think we have here Jeremy and Priyanka.
They can tell us a little bit more on how it's important
to make impact and help Microsoft products to succeed.
So let's start a little bit on the conversation here.
So tell me a little bit more.
Why don't you lead the MVP program recognition has brought
to you professionally, Jeremy?
Can you share a little bit more?
JEREMY SINCLAIR: Yes.
The MVP program has brought many opportunities
to me professionally.
It's fantastic to be recognized even
by other companies who've seen some of my contributions
through open source products.
I've been reached out to various companies
because they see my passion.
They know what I do because I talk about everything,
and I make sure that there is impact with my work.
FERNANDA SARAIVA: That's great.
BETSY WEBER: So as an MVP, do you have to write a blog?
JEREMY SINCLAIR: No.
You don't have to write a blog.
I mostly interact on socials.
So X, LinkedIn, BlueSky mostly.
But I rarely write blogs,
because I just put all my work on there.
BETSY WEBER: Priyanka, as an MVP,
do you have to run a user group?
PRIYANKA SHAH: Yes, we do.
And I think because the way we are pursued
as technology leaders in the community, the user groups
which we run, they make an impact in the sense
that we get an (inaudible) for technology sharing,
but then also we bring the community together.
And because right now AI is such a evolving, ever-changing space,
so which means these kinds of user groups,
meet up on a regular basis do help technologists get together,
give them a platform to learn, to share, and to grow.
BETSY WEBER: So as MVPs, Microsoft's always looking
for people that are passionate and they're doing what they love
and they're sharing their knowledge.
So we want you to give back to the community
in the ways you want to give back.
And I know Priyanka, you've run Agent Con and Agent Camp, right?
PRIYANKA SHAH: Yes.
BETSY WEBER: Why did you run these events?
PRIYANKA SHAH: Oh, perfect.
So as I said, because there's so much happening
in the technology space right now, and especially agentic AI,
agentic frameworks are the new buzzwords,
the new kids on the block.
And there's been so many people, students especially,
practitioners, and mid-level career people coming up to me
and asking, we hear a lot about agents, but then how to go
about (inaudible) agents?
Where do I start?
Where do I (inaudible) from my current workforce.
And which again got us to running this flagship events
which are (inaudible) global (inaudible) community,
and we are ambassadors in the global (inaudible) community.
We run country chapters or city chapters inside of a region.
So Agent Con (inaudible) global (inaudible) community was one
such a (inaudible) to then actually set up different types
of sessions just to clarify the agentic ecosystem.
And it was not just restricted to Microsoft Foundry.
So there are like, OpenClaw.
Then there's anthropic ecosystems.
So all of Microsoft
and Microsoft ecosystem partners clarifying the tools,
the practical use cases, what enterprises are doing.
So we had some of our clients come
and showcase how they are using agents
in their day-to-day enterprise workloads.
And that became sort of a platform for people
to understand agents, hygiene practices to build agents,
and Agent Con was about learning about agents.
And then the logical next step was Agent Camp, which was like,
okay, now you know agents.
Then come along and now start building agents.
Like, start learning how to build agents.
So one was like an introduction chapter, and then the next one,
the Agent Camp, which we did a couple of months ago was all
around getting your hands actually dirty
with building agentic ecosystems.
FERNANDA SARAIVA: That seems a lot of work.
I just got tired just listening to it, because I know
that that is a lot of passion evolving today,
and the more you pitch, the more you learn, and the more you want
to keep going and going.
And this is the main goal
of this program is just really make sure
that we are contributing to your system,
to your progress, to your evolution.
So then of course, you can just come back to us
and tell what is working, what is not working.
How can we actually prove a program?
So Jeremey, I believe you might be in the same,
similar route that Priyanka.
And that's a lot of work that you do.
So is that a lot (inaudible)?
How actually you do to actually balance your life, your work,
and your career, and your aspirations?
Tell us a little bit more,
like how is actually put all this passion together
into a single day?
JEREMY SINCLAIR: Yes.
So for me, I love to develop.
I have many ideas.
I have become an MVP for things that I use to kind of decompress
from a day and just I wanted to get excited.
So I've seen (inaudible) what can I look at?
What can I help out with?
And many times, I'm just thinking of things
in the back of my head.
Something that hasn't worked properly.
And so I'm like, alright, it's time to work on this.
I go looking through GitHub.
I go looking on socials.
And I see that there's someone having another issue.
So maybe I've found a workaround to it.
I go help them out, or I'll contribute to open source.
For example, one of my favorite repositories is the
PowerToys repository.
I bring this up because that -- yes, that repository --
this is for you, Clint --
repository brought me a lot of what people knew about.
And that's I ported PowerToys to run natively on ARM 64
because it didn't run on my Surface Pro S.
That was the core reason.
But then at the same time, I started learning more,
started interacting with the team.
And I started helping out and I learned things from them.
So it's great that I can give back and I can learn things,
and I can contribute to other spots.
I gain more confidence by giving back to community
and seeing the community interact.
So that's my Number 1 goal is to do what I can
to allow the community to feel comfortable
with getting out there.
BETSY WEBER: So you brought something, Jeremy,
you mentioned how it was rewarding,
the things you do in the community.
So as an MVP, there's several benefits to becoming one.
For instance, you have access to the product groups,
so you can share that feedback around those products
and services that you love and use.
There's also things like sneak peeks or previews
or you get information before the public gets
to learn about stuff.
What is the most rewarding part of being an MVP?
JEREMY SINCLAIR: The most rewarding part
of being MVP is you have that badge of honor and for me,
I have imposter syndrome.
So even every time it's time for renewal,
I'm thinking I'm not going to get this.
I'm not going to get this.
But then I look at what I've actually accomplished,
and I'm like you know what?
I can do this another year.
I can do this.
And so I start pinging up
yet another random project to work on.
And then I see the interaction with the Microsoft employees
who reach out and say hey,
we got (inaudible) preview for you to look at.
And it just so happens to tie in with something that I'm looking
at for an exploration.
And so there's feedback right there.
And so it was cool.
There was a few of those announcements that came
out today that I have been participating in.
FERNANDA SARAIVA: -- everything play in your mind.
JEREMY SINCLAIR: Oh yes.
FERNANDA SARAIVA: I want to do it.
I have my hands on it.
JEREMY SINCLAIR: Absolutely.
It's just so rewarding to be of use, because you get
that feedback, and you're not just another person.
FERNANDA SARAIVA: Yes.
And we tell, MVP program is available avenue,
because all those leaders are incredibly valuable
for Microsoft as well.
We praise every single bit of feedback,
every single experience from real work that you guys have
that is shared back to our products in the shape
of improvements, recognition, or a way to just --
even positive feedback.
"I love it; it works."
"I do not like it.
Maybe it should work this or this way."
So this whole machine of contribution and recognition
and it is exciting for Microsoft as well.
So we always like to understand how the community continue
to behave.
And one of the things that we always want to know,
if someone has never heard about communities, or anything,
why do you think it have actually the trigger
to start your career journey into the community?
Or start your journey into the community?
So what is this one thing that one day, you're just like, yes.
I want to engage in a community.
So Priyanka, how will you share your experience
about this topic?
PRIYANKA SHAH: So for me,
always came down to technology evangelism.
I'm a masters in data science,
and even before all this gen AI hype,
I was working towards upskilling,
reskilling students especially around AI, machine learning,
classic machine learning.
And I was doing it kind of (inaudible) casual way.
There was no channelizing
or like pinpointed user meetup groups, those kind of things.
So we just called it a casual coffee chats,
or how should I put it?
Like local meetups.
It was not community.
It was just evangelism in an already informal setting.
And then when I was approached for this kind of channelization
of the meetups which we do, and then the first time
and I was actually presenting on ml.net and actually doing a demo
and then actually enriching and looking at that feedback
and that satisfaction on the audience.
Oh, this is how it is done (inaudible) oh this is
something new.
This is how things would work.
And that kind of thing.
And I had that passion in me.
I think for people who want to get into this journey,
a community evangelism
or technology evangelism just does not mean speaking
at public events or as we say, upskilling, reskilling,
many of (inaudible) geeks who I know,
they do this technology sharing by blogs.
Writing. Maybe people do not have that kind
of public speaking (inaudible).
Could be very well.
They are happy doing their modes and codes.
But then a lot of people
who I know contribute using your GitHub checkin repositories,
(inaudible) requests, blogs,
technology reviews, writing books.
So that platform which you get,
which you can express your passion, that could be anything.
Public speaking, event organizing, even webinars,
seminars academic contributions.
So my point is pick your passion.
What are you passionate about?
And just start on that.
BETSY WEBER: I love that.
I think that's such great advice.
I hear from people, and they say do I have to do everything?
All the things?
And really to get the MVP Award, just follow your passion
and give back in a way that you want to give back.
So thank you.
That's great advice.
So now that you both have been MVPs for a while,
how has your professional or personal life changed
after receiving the MVP award?
JEREMY SINCLAIR: Well my personal and professional life,
I feel like I can walk with some swagger
because I have that MVP on me.
And I can say guess what?
I am the only Microsoft MVP
in the entire state of West Virginia.
I love to bring that up because, I know, thinking West Virginia,
most people see -- I don't know, they see a farm and that's that.
But this state has so much talent.
And I'm proof of that.
That's why I want everyone, if you have any idea,
or you think you can't do it, like I'm proof you can.
So Number 1 advice to anyone who wants to be
in this program, just keep your drive.
Don't think that whatever you're doing isn't enough.
Just keep at it and make sure that you're interacting
with others, interacting with the community.
Don't be afraid.
Just any little bit of contribution, that adds up.
PRIYANKA SHAH: For me, one of the important things is I work
in the consulting space.
I work in the system integration space.
So the MVP title, and especially (inaudible) specialization
like Foundry AI, that means my customers have a lot of trust
in what I'm communicating to them.
They also look up to us as technology leaders
who have a valid channel of communication
with Microsoft PMs and product groups.
Also that helps them bridge the gap between the current things
versus what is coming in future, what they should plan for.
Should they go live enterprise (inaudible)
or should they stop at a POC stage?
That's from a client perspective.
From my personal perspective, as I said, as this space grows,
I find myself more in the role of a mentor as well,
where I am trying to communicate all of these new skills, tools,
to the new generation, equipping them
to get themselves upskilled, reskilled for what is to come.
What are the kind of skills,
revolution we are seeing right now.
And I just think that it's passion.
So I don't feel that how I have an extra work.
Like we have hobbies (inaudible) for me it's
like a technology contribution.
Some community contribution.
So it's a passion.
I just love doing what I do.
FERNANDA SARAIVA: And this is what actually moves the needle.
Because those that if you don't know how to start sometimes,
that you're already doing community and they don't know.
By sharing with others, by contributing with others,
by playing with others in your company, in your group
of friends, by educating, maybe it's part of your profession.
So it's interesting to know the different experiences this way.
Especially for those that sometimes feel
like community is too much.
What do I actually need to do to become a community leader?
And I think I would love to --
we're just close to the end of this presentation.
I think we can just, both of you, you're just meeting someone
for the first time, just give your best remark of what means
for you, being an MVP.
Jeremy.
JEREMY SINCLAIR: What it means for me to be an MVP,
means that I've been chosen to be an MVP for a reason.
And so, like I said before, that brings me --
it makes me feel better as a person.
Makes me want to give back to the community.
It makes me want to keep growing,
both personally and professionally.
Getting all those professional relationships with others,
then keeping in communication.
The building future.
PRIYANKA SHAH: It's the mindshare which I get to how
with likeminded individuals globally.
And one advice I have to all the aspiring people
to join the MVP program is the program is just a benefit.
It's not your end goal.
The passion and contribution should stay.
The award just comes as an add-in.
So keep your passion, and that's it.
FERNANDA SARAIVA: That's awesome.
Thanks everyone.
Thanks for joining.
To learn more, aka.ms/MVP/learn.
So thank you.
[ Music ]
